how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Window replacement bid calculator

How much should I charge to replace windows?

Enough to cover the openings the house actually has, not enough to match the cheapest postcard on the block. A first-floor 3040 insert is not the same job as a second-floor 6048 picture window with a rotten sill, and a flat price per window cannot see the difference.

Open the free bid calculator

Price United Inches, not the count

Start with width and height on each opening, in inches. Add them. That sum is United Inches — the unit the glass shop prices from a stock 3040 (70 UI). A 6048 picture is 108 UI and is a different piece of glass, a different lift, and a different flash. Four identical bedrooms and one living-room picture are five openings on a postcard and two different invoices in the shop.

The second story is not “included”

A first-floor insert is a ladder and a helper. A second-floor bedroom is staging, a second pair of hands on the sash, and often a scaffold or a lift. A third-floor opening is a different day. If those hours are “included” in a $550-a-window special, they are unpaid. Count the story on every row.

Rot, masonry, and lead are a second labor list

A clean pocket install is one job. A sill that has to be cut out and rebuilt is carpentry. A brickmold cut-in is masonry time. A house built before 1978 is lead-safe work, not a free upgrade. Contractors who quote only the unit and “figure the rest in” are guessing the line that most often blows a postcard special.

Then load the wage and keep a margin

An installer paid $38 often costs more than $50 once employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability, and paid time off are counted. Overhead sits on top of that direct cost. Margin is a share of the price the customer sees, not a markup you add last and forget. The walk-away number is total cost: below it the job makes nothing, even before you pay yourself.

This is not a building-code price list

This is not a manufacturer size chart, not an Energy Star requirement, and not a finding that an opening is permitted, structurally sound, or lead-safe. The starting unit prices and hours are ballpark numbers so a contractor can see the shape of a bid. Replace them with the unit you buy and times from your own jobs, confirm measurements on site, and have a qualified professional review anything that has to be signed, inspected, or permitted.

Price this job in the calculator

Common questions

How much should I charge to replace windows?

Charge the openings the job will actually take — United Inches (width plus height) for the unit, plus hours for the story, the install method, and the tear-out — then divide cost by one minus your target margin. A flat price per window hides the difference between a first-floor 3040 insert and a second-floor 6048 picture window with a rotten sill.

What are United Inches on a window?

United Inches are width plus height in inches. A 3040 is 70 UI; a 6048 picture is 108 UI. Glass shops price from a stock 3040 and add for every extra inch. Labor also grows once the unit is no longer a one-person lift. Counting openings without counting UI is how two houses with the same window count produce different invoices.

Is this a building-code price list?

No. Starting unit prices and hours are editable ballpark numbers, not a manufacturer size chart, an Energy Star list, or a finding that any opening is permitted, structurally sound, or lead-safe. Confirm measurements and product quotes on site.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a manufacturer, building-code, Energy Star, lead, or insurance inspection. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Bid the opening, not the window.

A 3040 double-hung is not a 6048 picture window, a second-floor bedroom is not a first-floor insert, and a rotten sill is a carpentry job hiding inside a “window” line. A flat price per window cannot see any of that. Price United Inches, the story, and the tear-out — then see the walk-away number before a $550-a-window special eats the week.

Where the labor goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting unit prices and hours are common ballpark numbers, not a manufacturer size chart, an Energy Star list, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them. This is not a finding that any opening is permitted, structurally sound, or lead-safe.

    Common questions

    Why price by United Inches instead of per window?

    Because United Inches (width + height, in inches) is the unit the glass shop actually prices, and a flat per-window number cannot see it. Each opening's material starts from its type's base cost and adds a per-inch rate for every United Inch past a 70 UI baseline — roughly a stock 3040 double-hung. Labor gets a size step too: nothing extra up to 90 UI, about 0.45 h more past that, and about 1.1 h more past 120 UI. A 6048 picture window at 108 UI is not the same job as the 3040 the "$550 a window" postcard was written around.

    What's the difference between an insert and a full-frame replacement?

    An insert (pocket) leaves the existing frame in place and is the baseline here — no extra hours, no extra parts. Full-frame tears out to the studs, which adds about 1.4 h and $55 of material per opening. New-construction nail-fin sits between them at about 0.35 h and $28. The installation method is chosen per opening, so a house where three openings need full-frame and nine take inserts prices as the mixed job it is.

    How do rot, masonry, and pre-1978 lead work change the bid?

    They are opening-level conditions, each with their own hours and parts on top of the unit: sill or jamb rot repair adds about 1.8 h and $65, a masonry or brickmold cut-in about 1.6 h and $40, and lead-safe work practices on a pre-1978 house about 0.9 h and $48. These are ballpark starting figures for your own estimate, not a code requirement, an RRP compliance determination, or a finding that any particular opening contains lead — that is your inspection and your certification, not this page's.

    Why does the second story cost more when the window is the same?

    The unit is the same; the carry, the ladder, and the setup are not. A second-storey opening adds about 0.75 h and a third storey or higher about 2.1 h, per opening. Scaffolding or a lift is a separate flat cost, because it is a job-level rental decision rather than something that scales per window. Frame material scales the hours too — wood and clad-wood run about 20% slower than vinyl, fiberglass about 5%, aluminum slightly faster.

    Why does a small job still come out at a few hundred dollars?

    Because a one-window stop is mostly not the window. Round-trip drive time is priced from the miles and speed you enter, setup is its own line, there is a per-opening disposal figure for the old unit, and a minimum on-site hours floor applies when the real work comes in under it — a crew that shows up has a half-day gone whatever the takeoff says. Add the flat trip or truck fee and permits, and the floor for showing up is visible instead of buried.

    Why isn't a 20% margin the same as adding 20% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price — price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin) — which is how the quote reads to the customer and how your books read it. Overhead is a separate markup on the job's direct cost, applied before margin and never to itself or to profit. A $8,000 cost marked up 20% is $9,600 and only a 16.7% margin; a 20% target margin is $10,000. Nothing here or in the shareable link leaves your browser — the link carries your inputs in the URL, there is no account, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day.

vs-a-flat-price-per-window.html.text:
← Window Replacement Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per window

Window crews are shopped by a flat price per window. That rate cannot see the job — United Inches, story, frame, install method, and tear-out condition do not scale with a window count, and two jobs with the same number of openings can price over four times apart.

What a flat price per window is

A price per window is the fastest number to quote over the phone: count the openings, multiply by a rate, read back a total. It is also the unit homeowners already compare between competing bids, and the shape of the postcard special every crew gets shopped against.

The rate behind it was learned from a specific job — a given size, a given story, an insert into a clean opening — and then reused for the next window count that calls in, whether or not that next job shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter a per-opening takeoff — width and height in inches (United Inches), quantity, story, frame, install method, and tear-out condition — plus your own wage, payroll burden, travel, scaffolding, disposal, overhead, and target margin. It prices each opening's material and hours from its own size, story, frame, install method, and condition, not a rate carried over from the last job.

What a flat per-window rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a stock 3040 double-hung and a 6048 picture window, even though United Inches and material cost can differ several times over. Prices each opening's material from its type, frame, and United Inches past a 70 UI baseline, so a larger unit costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for story — a first-floor opening and a second-floor opening get the same rate. Adds ladder and setup hours per story, and prices scaffolding or a lift separately when any priced opening is on the second story or higher.
Has no line for install method — an insert that leaves the frame in place and a full-frame tear-out to the studs get the same rate. Prices insert, full-frame, and new-construction install methods as their own hours and material adders, per opening.
Has no line for condition — sill or jamb rot, a masonry cut-in, and pre-1978 lead-safe work are invisible inside a "window" line. Prices each condition as its own hours and parts, on top of the opening.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per opening and the walk-away price alongside the total, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same window count, two different jobs

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $32 hourly wage, 28% burden, 12 miles one way, $150 scaffolding when needed, $18 disposal per opening, 12% overhead, 25% target margin:

8 stock first-floor double-hung windows (30″×40″, 70 United Inches), installed as vinyl inserts into clean openings, take 15.6 crew-hours and price at $4,095.30 for the job — $511.91 per window.

The same 8 windows, but oversized second-floor wood casements (48″×64″, 112 United Inches), replaced full-frame with sill rot repair, plus interior casing and exterior capping on every opening, take 71.6 crew-hours, cost $14,107.24 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices the job at $18,809.65 — $2,351.21 per window. Quoting the harder job at the easy job's learned rate of $511.91 a window gives $4,095.30 for the same 8 openings, which is $10,011.94 below the harder job's own break-even cost — before counting the $14,714.35 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 25% target margin. Identical window count, more than four and a half times the labor, and a rate learned on the ground floor loses money the moment the crew opens the wall on the second.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per window get a replacement bid wrong?

Because a window count only measures how many openings there are, not what each one takes. 8 stock first-floor double-hung windows, installed as inserts in clean openings, take about 15.6 crew-hours. 8 oversized second-floor wood casements, replaced full-frame with sill rot repair plus interior casing and exterior capping, take about 71.6 crew-hours -- the same count of windows, more than four and a half times the labor, because United Inches, story, frame, install method, and condition do not scale with a window count.

What does a flat per-window rate usually miss entirely?

United Inches (a 6048 picture window is not the same material cost as a 3040 double-hung), story access (a second-floor opening adds ladder and setup time a first-floor opening does not), frame material (wood and clad-wood run slower and cost more than vinyl), install method (full-frame tear-out to the studs adds far more than an insert that leaves the frame in place), and condition (sill or jamb rot repair is a carpentry job hiding inside a "window" line). A flat rate has no line for any of them -- it is one number learned on one job and reused for the next window count that calls in.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs: 8 stock first-floor double-hung inserts take 15.6 crew-hours and price at $4,095.30 for the job -- $511.91 per window. 8 oversized second-floor wood casements, full-frame with rot repair plus interior casing and exterior capping, take 71.6 crew-hours, cost $14,107.24 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices the job at $18,809.65 -- $2,351.21 per window. Quoting the harder job at the easy job's learned rate of $511.91 a window gives $4,095.30 for the same 8 openings, which is $10,011.94 below the harder job's own break-even cost -- before counting the $14,714.35 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 25% target margin.

Is a flat price per window ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of similar openings -- the same size class, the same story, the same frame, an insert install, no rot -- a per-window number can land close. The risk is quoting an oversized unit, a second or third story, a full-frame tear-out, or sill rot the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know any of that until the crew opens the wall, and by then the per-window number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or unit prices?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supplier's unit pricing. It takes a per-opening takeoff with width, height, quantity, story, frame, install method, and condition, plus your own wage, payroll burden, travel, scaffolding, disposal, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into crew hours and a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-window rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Window Replacement Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read how much to charge to replace windows.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, supplier invoices, and a walk-through, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

vs-marketsharp.html.text:
← Window Replacement Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. MarketSharp

Two different shapes: MarketSharp is an account-based CRM for running a home-improvement company's whole lead-to-job pipeline. This page is a free, private, no-account worksheet for one number — whether the price for one window replacement job, priced correctly by United Inches, story, and tear-out, actually clears your cost and margin.

What each tool is for

MarketSharp is a cloud-based CRM and business-management platform built for the home-improvement and remodeling industry — window and door replacement, siding, and roofing contractors among its named markets. It is built around running a company's whole pipeline in one account: lead capture, appointment scheduling, estimating, customer communication, and reporting, used by a sales team and office staff together across every job the company runs, on an ongoing subscription. MarketSharp's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not track a lead, schedule an appointment, or hold a record across jobs. It takes one window replacement job — each opening's width and height converted to United Inches, story, frame material, install method (insert, full-frame, or new-construction), and tear-out condition such as rot, masonry cut-in, or pre-1978 lead work — and turns that into the job price, the price per opening, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to track leads, schedule appointments, and run reporting across every job my company sells.MarketSharp, or a comparable home-improvement CRM — running the whole pipeline is not something this calculator does.
Does the price for this one window replacement job actually clear my cost and target margin, once United Inches, story, and tear-out condition are counted correctly?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
What is the actual unit size for an opening, given its width and height — not a flat price-per-window number?This calculator's own United Inches takeoff.
I need my whole sales team working the same leads and estimates from one shared account.MarketSharp — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. MarketSharp's tools are used through a paid account.

Most window replacement contractors get different value from each: MarketSharp (or a comparable platform) for running the company's whole lead-to-job pipeline as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check on whether one job's price actually clears cost and margin before the bid goes out. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a project record or a lead-tracking system.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or MarketSharp?

They do different jobs. MarketSharp is a CRM and business-management platform built for home-improvement and remodeling contractors — windows, doors, siding, roofing, and similar exterior trades — to run a company's whole lead-to-job pipeline in one account: lead capture, scheduling, estimating, customer communication, and reporting, used by a sales team and office staff together across every job the company runs, on an ongoing subscription. This calculator does none of that. It takes one window replacement job — each opening's size in United Inches, story, frame, install method, and tear-out condition — and turns that into the job price, price per opening, effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal, instantly, in the browser, with no account and nothing uploaded. A company running leads and scheduling across many jobs at once is better served by MarketSharp or a comparable platform; a contractor who wants an instant, private, correctly-sized price for one job before a bid goes out is in the right place here.

Is this page affiliated with MarketSharp?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by MarketSharp. MarketSharp is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
